Every tool the MCP server exposes, grouped by bundle. This page says what a
bundle is, lists the bundles, finds any tool by name, and states the rules
every tool follows. Each bundle's page documents what its tools answer and
what they return.

This is lookup material, not reading material.

- [MCP server](@/docs/mcp.md) — what MCP is, and a first working example.
- [MCP deployment](@/docs/mcp-deploy.md) — the deployment shapes.
- [MCP protocol](@/docs/mcp-protocol.md) — the wire contract, security model and error semantics.


The v0.5 sipnab MCP tool surface. No tool edits the analysis in place, and
every response carries a ceiling.

That ceiling defaults to 1000 rows and is an
operator setting, not a build-time fact: `--mcp-max-rows N`, or `[limits]
mcp_max_rows` in the config file, with the flag winning. The right value
belongs to the consumer — a model with a small context window wants far fewer,
a batch client piping to a file wants far more. Note this is a DIFFERENT limit
from `dialog_limit`, which bounds dialogs tracked over the whole run and
defaults 100x higher.

One tool replaces
the analysis outright — `open_capture`, off unless you enable it — and it mints
a new capture identity so the replacement cannot reach a consumer as an
ordinary update.

## Bundles

A bundle is a named set of tools defined in sipnab's code. Every tool is in
exactly one bundle, so the ten bundles together are every tool the server has.
`--mcp-tools` loads bundles by name, as [Choosing which tools
load](#choosing-which-tools-load) describes, and each bundle has a page that
documents its tools.

| Bundle | Tools | What its tools answer |
|---|---|---|
| [`core`](@/docs/mcp-tools-core.md) | 9 | The smallest set that answers what happened on one call, and whether the fault was in signaling or media, from listing the calls to the bytes that prove it. |
| [`signaling`](@/docs/mcp-tools-signaling.md) | 20 | Follow-up questions about SIP signaling: single messages, call flows, SDP negotiation, related call legs, RFC conformance, time windows, and reproducing a call. |
| [`captures`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md) | 11 | Capture files in the file root: listing, searching, comparing, opening and exporting them, and the evidence that ties a finding to captured bytes. |
| [`security`](@/docs/mcp-tools-security.md) | 6 | Who sent what: scanner and fraud findings, the busiest sources, one endpoint's activity, registration problems, pass/fail expectations, and fail2ban rules. |
| [`media`](@/docs/mcp-tools-media.md) | 4 | Where a call's media endpoints came from, why a stream has no dialog, the facts under a quality score, and audio export. |
| [`relay`](@/docs/mcp-tools-relay.md) | 4 | Questions put to the configured media relay, and decoding the relay control messages sipnab captured. |
| [`tfps`](@/docs/mcp-tools-tfps.md) | 7 | The toll-fraud prevention peer (TFPS): what it blocks and logs, and the operator's ban, unban and revert actions. |
| [`server`](@/docs/mcp-tools-server.md) | 5 | The sipnab process and its capture path: capture health, HEP senders, resource use, build capabilities, and shutdown. |
| [`vcon`](@/docs/mcp-tools-vcon.md) | 5 | vCon conversation containers, exported, validated and analyzed, the vCon export spool's counts, and the SIPREC recording metadata a call carried. |
| [`tls`](@/docs/mcp-tools-tls.md) | 3 | Reading SIP inside TLS without keys through kernel uprobes, and which TLS libraries this host runs. |

### Choosing which tools load

Every tool the server registers sends its name, description and schemas to the
client on `tools/list`, and the client keeps them in the model's context for
the whole session. The client pays that cost before the agent asks anything, so
give a client that needs a few tools only those few:

```sh
sipnab -N -I capture.pcap --mcp --mcp-tools core,relay,get_sdp_timeline
```

`--mcp-tools` (or `[mcp] tools` in the [config file](@/docs/config.md#mcp))
takes a comma-separated list of:

- **bundles**, from the [bundle table](#bundles). Every tool is in exactly
  one, so the bundles together are `full`.
- **single tool names**, for one tool from a bundle you do not want whole.
- **your own bundles**, defined under `[mcp.bundles]` in the config file.
- **`full`**, every tool. This is the default.

sipnab refuses to start, exit 2, when a name is unknown or empty, and lists the
valid bundles. Names are case-sensitive. The handshake's `instructions` string
names the tools sipnab loaded and the bundles it left out, so an agent that misses a
tool can tell the operator which bundle holds it.

Output schemas are **off by default**. MCP makes them optional, and they are
more than half the bytes. Every response carries the same JSON with or without
them, as a text block and as `structuredContent`. Only a client that validates
responses against a declared shape needs them. Turn them on with
`--mcp-output-schemas` or `[mcp] output_schemas = true`.

To read one tool's response shape without turning output schemas on for every
tool, read the resource `sipnab://schema/<tool>`. It returns the tool's output
JSON Schema and an example payload generated from that schema, or says that
the tool declares no output schema.
[Tool response schemas](@/docs/mcp-protocol.md#tool-response-schemas) describes the
resource.

| Bundle | Tools | Bytes (default) | Bytes with output schemas |
|---|---|---|---|
| core | 9 | 12,223 | 54,526 |
| signaling | 20 | 22,349 | 58,494 |
| captures | 11 | 12,578 | 30,066 |
| security | 6 | 9,923 | 9,923 |
| media | 4 | 3,480 | 16,048 |
| relay | 4 | 4,240 | 20,029 |
| tfps | 7 | 5,563 | 15,947 |
| server | 5 | 5,394 | 27,170 |
| vcon | 5 | 8,369 | 24,354 |
| tls | 3 | 2,850 | 4,943 |
| full | 74 | 86,969 | 261,500 |

Bytes are the compact JSON of each tool's `tools/list` entry, summed over the
bundle.

> **Measured after sipnab 0.5.212** on a build with every feature, with
> `max_response_bytes` and the `get_dialog` and `reconcile_orphans` cursors,
> output schemas on nine `core` and `signaling` tools, the response limits and
> loaded-surface fields of `server_capabilities`, and `vcon_spool_status` and
> the `cursor` and `media` parameters of `export_vcon` in place, and the `vcon`
> and `full` rows measured again once `analyze_vcon` joined them. Sizes, tool
> counts and bundle membership may change in later releases. A build without a
> feature does not register that feature's tools, so its bundles are smaller.
> The test `each_bundle_stays_within_its_byte_budget` fails when a bundle grows
> past its recorded ceiling; update this table in the same change.

A snapshot of files; sends, moves and deletes nothing |

## Which tool finds calls

Seven tools select calls, and each answers a different question. A filter is
an expression in sipnab's filter language (the DSL), such as
`state == failed`, or the name of a built-in alias such as `problems`.

| The question | The tool | Why this one |
|---|---|---|
| Which calls match this condition? | [`list_dialogs`](@/docs/mcp-tools-core.md#list-dialogs) with `filter` | Takes an alias or any DSL expression and pages through every match, with `total_matched` and a cursor |
| Which calls show a known kind of problem? | [`find_problems`](@/docs/mcp-tools-core.md#find-problems) | Takes diagnostic alias names (`problems`, `slow-setup`, `one-way` and the rest) instead of an expression, and can narrow them with a DSL filter |
| Which calls contain this text: a number, a User-Agent, a header value? | [`search_messages`](@/docs/mcp-tools-core.md#search-messages) | Searches the whole SIP message, every header, the request line and the body, case-insensitively, and returns the message that matched |
| Which calls started in this time window? | [`search_by_time`](@/docs/mcp-tools-signaling.md#search-by-time) | Selects by the time of the first message, in an [RFC 3339](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc3339) window, optionally narrowed by a filter |
| What did this one IP address or user do? | [`describe_endpoint`](@/docs/mcp-tools-security.md#describe-endpoint) | Selects by `ip` or `user` and returns counts over every match plus a page of that participant's dialogs |
| Which capture file holds these calls? | [`find_in_captures`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#find-in-captures) | Sweeps the files in `--mcp-file-root` with a filter and names the files that match, without replacing the loaded capture |
| Does my filter parse, and how many calls does it select? | [`validate_filter`](@/docs/mcp-tools-signaling.md#validate-filter) | Compiles the expression and returns the count with no rows, so a wrong filter costs one small answer |

## Prompts

A prompt is a named list of steps that tells a model which tools to call and
in what order. A client lists them with `prompts/list` and fetches one with
`prompts/get`. No prompt takes arguments, and every tool stays callable
without one.

| Prompt | When to use it | Tools it calls, in order | Bundles it needs |
|---|---|---|---|
| `triage-outage` | Something is failing now | `capture_status`, `find_problems`, `triage_call`, `show_evidence` | `core`, `captures` |
| `carrier-escalation` | Building a case to send to a carrier | `capture_status`, `group_dialogs`, `get_call_tree`, `build_evidence_package` | `core`, `signaling`, `captures` |
| `codec-interop-audit` | Two endpoints disagree about media | `capture_status`, `check_codec_negotiation`, `group_dialogs`, `media_diagnostics` | `core`, `signaling`, `media` |
| `post-change-verification` | A change went in and needs checking against a baseline | `capture_status`, `compare_captures`, `evaluate_expectations`, `timeline` | `core`, `signaling`, `captures`, `security` |
| `vcon-handoff` | You are exporting calls to a vCon store | `capture_status`, `validate_filter`, `export_vcon`, `validate_vcon` | `core`, `signaling`, `vcon` |

Each prompt's steps:

- **`triage-outage`**: read `unanalysed_sip_messages` from `capture_status`
  first; get the shape of the failure from `find_problems`; run `triage_call`
  on one Call-ID from that result; follow its `frame` pointer with
  `show_evidence` before stating that a message caused the failure.
- **`carrier-escalation`**: `capture_status`; `group_dialogs` by `next_hop`
  with the `asr` and `ner` metrics, reading the `population` block;
  `get_call_tree` on an affected Call-ID, because carrier faults usually span
  several legs; `build_evidence_package` for the calls the escalation cites.
- **`codec-interop-audit`**: `capture_status`; `check_codec_negotiation` for
  offers with no common codec; `group_dialogs` by `rtp.codec` with `mos_p10`;
  `media_diagnostics` on a call that negotiated a codec and still sounded
  wrong.
- **`post-change-verification`**: `capture_status`; `compare_captures`
  against the baseline from before the change; `evaluate_expectations` when the
  repository has a rules file; `timeline` to check the failures did not move
  to a different hour.
- **`vcon-handoff`**: `capture_status`; `validate_filter` on the filter that
  selects the calls; `export_vcon` with that `filter`; `validate_vcon` on each
  exported container, passed as `container`; then record each container's
  `digest` (its SHA-256) and Call-ID. Passing `call_id` to `validate_vcon`
  instead exports a second container with a different creation time, so its
  digest differs from the one sent.

**sipnab serves a prompt only when the server registers every tool it
calls.** Under `--mcp-tools core`, `prompts/list` returns no prompt, because
each one calls at least one tool outside `core`. `prompts/get` refuses a prompt
it does not serve with error -32602, and the message names the tools the
server does not register and the bundles that hold them. sipnab hides the prompt rather than
serving it with a note, because a step that names a tool the client cannot call
fails with "tool not found" in the middle of the workflow. A tool counts as
loaded when the server registers it, so a tool the build does not carry also
hides the prompts that call it.

## Rules every tool follows

Seven rules hold across the whole surface. Each tool section on a bundle page
states only what its tool does differently, so read these once and skip them
afterwards.

**A required parameter has no default.** Leave one out, or send the wrong JSON
type, and the call fails with `invalid_params` (-32602) before the tool runs.
Optional parameters carry a `?` in every parameter table, and each row says
what the tool does when you omit that one.

**A `limit` of `0` means the default, not "no rows".** `limit` defaults to 50
everywhere it appears. The server clamps anything larger to `--mcp-max-rows`
(1000 unless the operator lowered it) and returns the clamped page without an
error. Both edges bite the same caller: a client that computes `limit` from
"rows I still want" asks for 50 when it meant to ask for none, and a client
that asks for 5000 to "get everything" receives 1000 and no complaint. Read
`returned` rather than the length you asked for.

**Pass a cursor back exactly as it arrived.** `next_cursor` pairs a timestamp
with an identity — `<RFC 3339>|<Call-ID>` for dialogs,
`<RFC 3339>|<Call-ID>#<message index>` for `search_messages` hits and
`get_dialog` messages, and `<RFC 3339>|0xSSRC@src>dst` for the `rtp_stats`
sweep and `reconcile_orphans`. A hand-rebuilt bare timestamp still parses on
the dialog tools, so rebuilding one costs rows instead of raising an error.
`next_cursor: null` marks the final page.

**A page ends at the first bound it reaches, and says which.** Two bounds
apply to every paged tool: the row limit (`limit`, clamped to
`--mcp-max-rows`) and the byte budget (`max_response_bytes`, clamped to
`--mcp-max-response-bytes`, 1048576 bytes unless the operator changed it).
Either one sets `truncated: true`, names itself in `truncated_by` — `rows` or
`bytes` — and leaves a `next_cursor` that resumes at the first row the page
left out. `truncated_by` is absent when neither bound cut the page. The byte budget drops
whole rows from the end of the page and never part of one, and a page always
keeps at least one row, so following the cursor always moves forward even when
one row alone is larger than the budget. It counts the bytes the
`sipnab_mcp_tool_response_bytes_total` metric counts: the JSON page, the
provenance note and the two completeness booleans below. The JSON-RPC framing
and the `structuredContent` copy of the page are not counted. Every paged tool
takes it: `list_dialogs`, `find_problems`, `search_by_time`, `search_messages`,
`tail_dialogs`, `get_dialog`, `reconcile_orphans` and the `rtp_stats` sweep.

**Every list-style tool answers with a page object, never a bare array.** The
rows sit under a named key — `dialogs`, `hits`, `streams`, `findings` — beside
`returned` and `total_matched`, so counting the rows is never necessary and
never right. `search_messages` and `security_findings` carry the
page fields too. `tail_dialogs` is the one page object with no
total, because a tail cannot have one. [Response
bounding](#response-bounding) tabulates it.

**Every answer says how much of the capture is behind it.** Two booleans ride
on every response object: `source_exhausted`, true once sipnab has read the
source to its end, and `source_stopped_early`, true when a read ended before the
source did — a truncated dump file, a file that would not open, a read error
part-way through. The answer is the WHOLE answer only when `source_exhausted` is
true and `source_stopped_early` is false, and one response tells you that much,
so nothing has to call `capture_status` to interpret it.

Until then the response omits `truncated: false` entirely. That value claims
outright that the page holds every match, and a caller reading only that field
deserves no claim rather than a wrong one — JSON absence and `false` are
different values. The response still says `truncated: true` whenever the row cap
really did keep matches out, because that fact holds whatever the load state.
`complete`, where a tool has one, likewise never reads `true` over a partial
read.

A file source loads on a background thread, so an agent's first call lands
inside a window a human client never sees: on a 921 MB capture, `list_dialogs`
answered with 6 of 18,241 dialogs. `tail_dialogs` and `capture_status` have
always carried `source_exhausted`. Now every tool that answers from the capture
does.

Nineteen tools are the exception, because their answer cannot move with
the load. Eleven read something other than the capture store —
`explain_response_code`, `explain_rule`, `decode_evidence`, `decode_ng`,
`show_evidence`, `list_captures`, `list_tls_libraries`, `server_capabilities`,
`vcon_spool_status`, which counts the vCon export spool that the forwarder
drains, `compare_captures`, which reads two files and never the loaded
capture, and `analyze_vcon`, which analyzes a container the caller hands over.
The other eight ask another process: `query_relay` and `relay_stats` put the
question to the media relay, and `tfps_status`, `tfps_banned`, `tfps_dropped`,
`tfps_labels`, `tfps_ban` and `tfps_unban` put it to the toll-fraud prevention
peer. How much
of the capture sipnab has read says nothing about what those hold.

The
tools that answer with a rendered document — `render_ladder`, and
`get_capture_report` / `get_dialog_report` in `markdown` and `text` — have no
object to put a field in, so they say it in prose instead: a document drawn
over a capture that is still loading, or over one whose read stopped before its
end, ends with the same `INCOMPLETE RUN` block `--report` appends, naming each
reason. A document drawn over a capture read in full says nothing extra,
because a caveat on every answer is a caveat nobody reads.

Every other tool answers with a JSON object, so the two booleans sit in the
object beside the tool's own fields — [`timeline`](@/docs/mcp-tools-signaling.md#timeline) was the last one
returning a bare array, and it now wraps its rows in an object for exactly this
reason.

**Capture text arrives fenced, and identifiers do not.** Free text an endpoint
wrote — display names, `User-Agent`, SDP, whole messages — comes wrapped in
`⟦untrusted-capture-data⟧` … `⟦/untrusted-capture-data⟧`, and the tools that
emit it append a provenance note as the LAST content block. Call-IDs, cursors,
addresses and timestamps stay verbatim so they pass straight into the next
call. [Untrusted capture text](@/docs/mcp-protocol.md#untrusted-capture-text) gives the per-tool
breakdown. Every JSON sample on the bundle pages shows the markers where the
server really emits them.

### Narrowing a row with `fields`

`list_dialogs`, `find_problems`, `tail_dialogs` and `search_by_time` take an
optional `fields` array. This surface already bounds rows three ways -- `limit`, `--mcp-max-rows`, and
cursors -- and it bounded columns not at all, so asking for a page to read two
values off it still paid for every other value on every row.

```jsonc
// list_dialogs { "limit": 200, "fields": ["state", "final_status_code"] }
{ "call_id": "1-1966@10.0.2.20", "state": "Completed", "final_status_code": 200 }
```

Three rules, each there for a reason:

- **`call_id` always survives**, listed or not. Every follow-up tool here takes
  a Call-ID, so a row an agent cannot address is a row it can do nothing with.
- **An unknown name fails**, naming both the typo and the fields the row
  actually carries. Silently returning rows without the field asked for reads
  as "no such data", which is a wrong answer rather than an error.
- **The envelope is never projected.** `total_matched`, `truncated`,
  `next_cursor` and `capture_identity` are how a caller knows what it did NOT
  get, and dropping them to save bytes would trade away the very thing the
  bounds exist to report.

A field already absent from a row stays absent rather than reappearing as
null: the projection runs on the serialized page, so `skip_serializing_if`
still decides what exists.

### File tools — the shared rule

`list_captures`, `export_capture`, `export_audio`,
[`compare_captures`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#compare-captures) and
[`build_evidence_package`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#build-evidence-package) all require
`--mcp-file-root <DIR>` and refuse to run without it. They take a **bare
filename, never a path**. [`generate_repro`](@/docs/mcp-tools-signaling.md#generate-repro) joins them the
moment you give it a `filename`, and
[`decode_evidence`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#decode-evidence) pushes the source half of a frame pointer
through the same guard.

sipnab refuses `../x`, `/etc/passwd` and `sub/dir.pcap` before any filesystem
call. That is the whole security model and it is deliberately absolute: a tool
accepting an agent-supplied path is an arbitrary file write, not an export.

Name checking alone does not finish the job, so sipnab does one more thing. A
symlink already sitting in the root is a single bare component — it passes every
check above, and the kernel follows it when the file opens. sipnab therefore
compares the resolved path against the root in its fully resolved form and refuses a name by
where it points rather than by how someone spelled it. Each tool returns the
resolved path, so a caller learns where the bytes actually went.

That escape needed prior write access inside the root, so it never amounted to a
remote break. sipnab closes it because this reference calls the boundary absolute, and
a boundary described that way ought to be.

> **The boundary stops an escape, and an overwrite.** Inside the root,
> `export_capture`, `export_audio`, `build_evidence_package`, `generate_repro`'s
> `filename` and `shutdown_server`'s `save_to` refuse a
> filename that already exists, name the file, and ask for one that is free.
> sipnab declines to write over a file it did not create, because that file may
> hold the only copy of a capture. Call
> [`list_captures`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#list-captures) to see which names a directory already
> uses.
>
> The guard covers every capture in the root, not only the one the run is
> reading. Narrowed to the current capture it would miss the others staged
> there for [`open_capture`](@/docs/mcp-tools-captures.md#open-capture), and every earlier export, which
> then fall to a name collision on a call that reports success.

### Tool argument enums

**`find_problems.kinds`** — diagnostic alias names, OR-ed together.
Defaults to `["problems"]`. The full vocabulary:

`problems` · `slow-setup` · `short-calls` · `one-way` · `nat-issues` ·
`codec-asym` · `ptime-asym` · `payload-asym` · `duration-asym` ·
`late-media`

An unknown alias returns a JSON-RPC *invalid params* error naming the
bad alias. The same names work as the `list_dialogs` `filter` aliases
(and as `sipnab --filter` aliases on the CLI).

**`security_findings.kinds`** — matches the rule names sipnab records
findings under: `scanner`, `fraud`, `digest`, `reg_flood` (note the
underscore — the `--alert` rule grammar spells it `reg-flood`, but
sipnab records and filters findings as `reg_flood`). Omitted or empty
`kinds` returns findings of every kind.

Both enums **refuse** a name they do not know, and name the vocabulary in the
refusal. `security_findings.kinds` used to accept anything and match nothing,
so a name outside those four answered `[]` — the same bytes a quiet capture
returns. `reg-flood` was the case that bit, and its refusal now suggests the
underscore spelling by name.

### Error model

All tools return MCP errors via the JSON-RPC `error` object. The codes
sipnab uses:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| -32602 (`invalid_params`) | Unknown Call-ID, out-of-range index, malformed filter, unknown format, unknown alias, a path where a bare filename belongs, and every "this tool is not enabled" refusal. The common case by far. |
| -32603 (`internal_error`) | A read or write that reached the filesystem or the decoder and failed there — `export_audio` with no retained payload, a capture file sipnab cannot open. Not only for bugs. |
| -32000 (server error) | Capacity, not correctness: `--mcp-max-concurrent` or `--mcp-rate-limit-per-peer` turned this call away, and the same call succeeds once the server has room. The only code here worth a retry — treat -32602 as a bug in the request. |

Tools never panic. An unknown Call-ID always produces a structured error
rather than an empty result.

#### Error data

Every -32602 and -32000 error also carries a `data` object, so a client can act
on the error without parsing `message`. The `message` text stays as it was.
People read `message`, and its wording may improve between releases. The
`data` codes below stay stable.

```jsonc
{
  "code": -32602,
  "message": "cannot group by 'bogus'; one of: state, response_code, ...",
  "data": {
    "reason": "invalid_choice",       // always present
    "param": "group_by",              // the argument that was refused, when one was
    "valid_values": ["state", "response_code", "method", "..."]  // the allowed set, when there is one
  }
}
```

| Member | Present | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `reason` | always | A stable lowercase code from the table below. |
| `param` | when one argument caused the refusal | The argument's name, as the tool's input schema spells it. For a resource read, the URI template variable (`tool`, `alias`, `rule_id`) or `uri`. |
| `valid_values` | when the refusal is "not one of these" | The values the server accepts for that argument. |
| `retry_after_ms` | on a rate-limit refusal | Milliseconds until the current one-second window ends and the same call can succeed. |

sipnab omits a member that does not apply, rather than sending it as `null`.

| `reason` | Code | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `not_found` | -32602 | A named thing (a Call-ID, a rule, a finding, a sweep job, a subscription) is not held by this server. |
| `invalid_choice` | -32602 | The value is not in the allowed set; `valid_values` lists the set. |
| `invalid_value` | -32602 | The value is empty, out of range, or not in the expected format. |
| `invalid_filter` | -32602 | A filter expression did not compile. |
| `missing_param` | -32602 | A required argument, or one of a set of alternatives, was not given. |
| `conflicting_params` | -32602 | The call named two arguments that cannot appear together. |
| `not_enabled` | -32602 | The operator did not enable this on the server: an opt-in flag such as `--mcp-allow-shutdown`, `--mcp-file-root`, or `--allow-action`. |
| `path_refused` | -32602 | sipnab refused a filename: not a bare name, outside `--mcp-file-root`, or one of the capture's own inputs. |
| `already_exists` | -32602 | The filename asked for already exists, and sipnab does not overwrite. |
| `not_ready` | -32602 | The server's current state refuses the request (a capture is still loading, a live capture is running, the source has not finished). The same call can succeed later. |
| `limit_exceeded` | -32602 | The request asks for more than a ceiling this server enforces. |
| `unsupported` | -32602 | This build, platform, or process privilege cannot do this. |
| `scope_refused` | -32602 | The caller's token scope does not cover this tool. |
| `declined` | -32602 | The person asked to confirm the request (MCP elicitation) declined it. |
| `no_data` | -32602 | The named call holds nothing of the kind asked for: no messages, no RTP streams, no request to replay. |
| `unknown_tool` | -32602 | The tool name is not loaded on this server; `valid_values` lists the loaded names. |
| `invalid_arguments` | -32602 | An argument this server refuses whatever its value (a password-like argument name), or a refusal the MCP SDK built without naming the argument. |
| `at_capacity` | -32000 | `--mcp-max-concurrent` calls are already running. There is no `retry_after_ms`, because a slot frees when some running call ends and the server cannot know when that happens. |
| `rate_limited` | -32000 | This peer used its `--mcp-rate-limit-per-peer` allowance for the current one-second window. `retry_after_ms` says when the window ends. |

The MCP SDK answers arguments that do not match a tool's input schema at all
(a wrong JSON type, a missing required key) with a tool result that has
`isError: true` and the parse error as its text, not with a JSON-RPC error, so
that answer carries no `data`.

### Response bounding

| Limit | Default | Set by |
|---|---|---|
| Default `limit` for list-style tools | 50 | the per-call `limit` |
| Ceiling on `limit` (clamps higher requests) | 1000 | `--mcp-max-rows` |
| SIP body / snippet bytes | 4096 | `--mcp-max-body-bytes` |
| Messages per `get_dialog` page | 1000 | `--mcp-max-rows` |
| Bytes of one whole paged response | 1048576 | the per-call `max_response_bytes`, up to `--mcp-max-response-bytes` |

**These are defaults, not laws.** The right ceiling belongs to the CONSUMER
rather than to sipnab: an agent with a small context window wants far fewer
than a thousand rows and a batch consumer piping to a file wants far more, so
no single number serves both. Raise or lower them with `--mcp-max-rows`,
`--mcp-max-body-bytes` and `--mcp-max-response-bytes`, or the matching
`[limits]` keys in the config file. The per-call `limit` and
`max_response_bytes` narrow an answer below the ceiling, and cannot exceed it.

The row and body ceilings bound a row's count and a body's width, and neither
bounds the response as a whole: fifty `get_dialog` messages that each carry a
long SDP body are within both and can still exceed what a small model can read.
The byte budget covers that case. Its default of 1048576 bytes (1 MiB) is under
twice the largest response measured over the sample captures in
`tests/pcap-samples` — 561,420 bytes, `list_dialogs` with `limit: 1000` on
`sipp-branch-scenario.pcapng` — so with the default no answer on those captures
changes. The largest at the default `limit` was 52,809 bytes, a `get_dialog`
page on `DTMFsipinfo.pcap`.

A bound is not a loss. `list_dialogs`, `find_problems`, `search_by_time`,
`search_messages`, `security_findings` and the capture-wide `rtp_stats` sweep
each report `total_matched` beside their page, so a caller sees how much of the
answer it holds.

That number describes the STORE, not the file: while the
source is still loading it counts what had arrived by then, which is why every
one of them also carries `source_exhausted` and why the response omits
`truncated: false` until the answer is whole.

All of those except `security_findings` carry a cursor to the rest, as do
`tail_dialogs`, `get_dialog` and `reconcile_orphans`, and every one of the eight
cursor tools takes `max_response_bytes`. Asking for a `limit` above the ceiling
does nothing — the ceiling clamps it — so either raise the ceiling with
`--mcp-max-rows` or page.

**Some tools take `limit` and carry no cursor, and a caller has to know
which:**

| Tool | Reports a total | Why no cursor | How to reach the rest |
|---|---|---|---|
| `security_findings` | Yes, `total_matched` | Its source is a ring buffer whose default depth is 1000, the same as the maximum `limit`, so one call reaches all of it | Raise `limit`, and narrow with `since` |
| `find_correlated` | Yes, `total_matched` | A ranking by score: a later page would hold weaker matches, not the rest of a list | Raise `limit` |
| `get_call_tree` | No, `truncated` only | A breadth-first walk outward from one call, stopped at `limit` legs | Raise `limit` |
| `top_talkers` | Yes, `distinct_talkers` | A ranking by dialog count | Raise `limit` |
| `describe_endpoint` | Yes, `dialogs` | `recent_dialogs` is newest first by `updated_at`, which moves each time a call gains a message, so a cursor on it would skip rows | [`list_dialogs`](@/docs/mcp-tools-core.md#list-dialogs) with a filter such as `src.ip == '192.0.2.10'` or `from.user == 'alice'` pages that endpoint's dialogs |
| `hep_senders` | Yes, `senders_tracked` and `refused_sources_tracked` | Two lists in one answer, the refused sources ranked by count, and the same bytes `GET /v1/hep/senders` returns | Raise `limit`, and raise `--mcp-max-rows` as well when the listener tracks more than 1000 senders |
| `tfps_labels` | No: `total` counts the rows TFPS returned, and `truncated` says it held more | TFPS's `log` command takes a row count and no offset, so there is no position to resume from | Raise `limit`, or run `tfps_ctl log --json --limit N` on the TFPS host |
| `tail_dialogs` | No | It has a cursor. The table names it because it has no total | Follow `next_cursor` until the page comes back empty |

`aggregate_dialogs`, `group_dialogs` and `compare_captures` take `top_n` rather
than `limit` and sum everything past it into `other_count` or `other`, so they
withhold nothing silently and have no cursor either. `tail_dialogs` reports no
total because a tail cannot have one: the store keeps changing underneath it,
so any number it gave would describe a moment that has passed.

## Reproduce the examples

Each tool section on a bundle page names the capture its example ran against.
Start a server on that capture, then call the tool. These two cover most of
the examples:

```bash
# The paging examples: 1334 dialogs, no RTP.
sipnab -N --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 \
       --mcp-file-root tests/pcap-samples \
       -I tests/pcap-samples/sipp-branch-scenario.pcapng
```

```bash
# The media examples: one completed call, two RTP streams.
sipnab -N --mcp --mcp-transport http --mcp-bind 127.0.0.1:8731 \
       --mcp-file-root tests/pcap-samples \
       -I tests/pcap-samples/sip-rtp-g711.pcap
```

Drive either one with the [raw HTTP test](@/docs/mcp-deploy.md#test-the-http-wire-by-hand) on the deployment page, or point
a client at `http://127.0.0.1:8731/mcp`. A loopback bind needs no token.

Numbers in the samples are what those captures produce. Jitter and MOS come out
byte-identical run to run, because a file replay reads packet timestamps rather
than arrival times, so a value that fails to match points at a real change
rather than at timing noise.
